I have noticed much huffing and puffing in the media that Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new press secretary, supposedly lied when claiming to be a "lawyer." Actually, she is a lawyer. But she is apparently not an attorney.

item.title: I Stand Corrected
item.description: Well, this has been fun. item.content:encoded:
Well, this has been fun.

When the media hysteria erupted over Katie Zacharia’s claim that she’s a “lawyer,” I recalled learning some years ago that there is a technical distinction between “attorney” and “lawyer.” As I noted, the terms are often used interchangeably these days. But I thought she was not wrong to label herself a “lawyer” since, as I understood it, “lawyer” applies to someone who has completed a legal education, and Zacharia earned a JD from Pepperdine Law School. I also noted that she could not claim to be an attorney, since she is not licensed in any jurisdiction.

To be sure that my recollection was correct, I looked into the question and found many sources stating that very thing. Here’s one. There are plenty more. I also asked AI to verify. It did. Perhaps it was the way I phrased the inquiry.

I have since been barraged with many angry tirades on social media. Some people run on rage, I guess.

But some were substantive responses, which I appreciate because I always want to be accurate. I am especially thankful to Shannen W. Coffin for his informed rebuttal (and kind words). To say the least, my assertion that Zacharia is “unquestionably” a lawyer is, as the old Watergate phrase had it, “no longer operative.” Clearly, some jurisdictions have erased that (perhaps now archaic) technical distinction by statute.

I wrote about this — which is outside of my usual areas of concern — because I am growing weary of the mainstream media’s many moral panics that heap vituperation on people’s heads, often for very little cause. And since Zacharia is not going to provide legal advice or counsel in her role at the White House, I thought the controversy over her past biographical statements to be “much ado about very little.” I mostly still do.

But: I also believe that Jim Geraghty’s concerns about Zacharia’s work in China are well founded. She owes the country a deeper explanation (assuming she survives in the job).

In summary, I stand corrected.

Now, back to our regularly scheduled programming.

item.title: Nature Article Denies AI Consciousness
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
I am so used to ideologically extreme and transgressive articles published in science and other professional journals, that when one publishes commonsense commentary, I think it should be applauded.

As most readers know, there is a great advocacy push underway to have AI declared to be — or soon to be — conscious and hence, entitled to “rights” as “persons.” (I have responded to this advocacy on several occasions.) Now, an article in Nature — written by three academics — strongly rebuts that blatant anthropomorphism.  From “Three Reasons Why AI Is Not Conscious and Perhaps Never Will Be:

Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies.

Pet peeve: They really mean they “think” that AI consciousness is unlikely, not that they “feel” it. Those concepts are not the same and that matters. I think — ha — that we should stop conflating the two.

Back to the article. The professors list three reasons for their assertion. First, they distinguish between “intelligence” and “consciousness”:

Intelligence is not consciousness: What we mean by consciousness is simple enough: it is what goes away with dreamless sleep or under general anaesthesia, and what returns after waking up or while dreaming. Conscious experiences feel like something, whether it is tasting ice cream on a hot day or seeing the vibrant colours of a sunset…

This definition of consciousness introduces the first reason for scepticism about conscious AI. Consciousness is not the same thing as intelligence. Consciousness is about being and feeling; intelligence — very broadly — is all about doing, or performing functions. Just because something is intelligent does not mean that it is conscious…

Second. The human brains is not merely “an information-processing device”:

Silicon brains: The idea of conscious AI is motivated by the assumption that algorithms running on silicon are, in principle, sufficient for consciousness. In other words, that computation of the right kind is all that it takes, and that it doesn’t matter whether these computations are implemented inside carbon-based brains or in silicon-based computers. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. Although computations are clearly sufficient to produce forms of intelligence — as modern AI systems demonstrate — it is much less clear that they could also be sufficient for consciousness.

Computational functionalism is widely assumed among members of the tech community and is popular among some scientists and philosophers, too, but we think it is fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat.

The third considers two theories of consciousness that require living tissue as a predicate for consciousness:

These proposals are all forms of biological naturalism: the view that biological properties are necessary for consciousness. Pulling all this together, the balance of theory and evidence strongly suggests that, no matter how intelligent it is, silicon-based AI is unlikely to be or become conscious.

The authors conclude:

The default position of the research community should therefore be that AI is not conscious and should not be treated as such.

In our view, silicon, digital AI systems should be considered objects, not subjects; they are smart tools, not smart people. Advocating that current AI systems should have rights and welfare protection is not just mistaken, it diverts attention and scarce resources away from where they belong: dedicated to the well-being of fellow sentient beings.

Bravo. I think much more could and should be said about this. But good on the editors of Nature for pushing back against the subversive notion that a machine can be the moral equivalent of a human being.
